notes.kiddugavu: For eki- nouns. The root is -dugavu.
notes.kyeru: For eki- nouns. The root is -eru.
notes.kiragala: Use with kya/ya: ekitabo kya kiragala.
notes.kyenvu: For eki- nouns. The root is -yenvu.
notes.bbulu: From English. Use with kya/ya: kya bulu.
notes.kitaka: Literally “soil”. Use with kya/ya: ya kitaka.

notes.kibi: For eki- nouns. The root is -bi.

guidebook.intro: Describing words in Lusoga follow the noun, and they wear the noun’s class prefix. Learn the root once and you can describe anything.

tips.title: Two kinds of colour word
body: Some colours are adjectives with a root that takes the noun’s prefix: **-myufu** (red), **-dugavu** (black), **-eru** (white) and **-yenvu** (yellow). With an **eki-** noun they become **kimyufu**, **kidugavu**, **kyeru**, **kyenvu**.
Others are nouns, so you say “of green”: **kya kiragala**, **kya bulu**, **kya kakobe**. The **kya** changes with the class too: **emeeza ya kitaka** (a brown table).

tips.title: Saying “is” and “the red one”
body: To say a thing **is** big, put the adjective after the noun with no initial vowel: **Ekibuga kinene** (the town is big).
To describe it inside a sentence, keep the initial vowel: **ekikopo ekimyufu** (the red cup). **Njagala ekikopo ekimyufu** means “I want the red cup”.

tips.title: Describing people
body: People take **mu-** for one person and **ba-** for many, just like **omuntu** and **abantu**. The same roots you used for things work here.

culture.title: Mukade is a compliment
body: Calling an elder **mukade** (old one) is respectful, not rude. Age brings standing, and the word **abakade** (the elders) is used for respected senior people in a family or village.

culture.title: Kirungi, the all-purpose word
body: **Kirungi** (it’s good) is one of the most useful words you’ll hear: to agree, to approve, to say “that’s fine”. **Kirungi nnyo!** is “excellent!”.
